 Prediction markets have soared during Trump's second term, but allowing betting on elections puts top apps in the crosshairs of politicians. 
 Design by Grace Hughes, Photos by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images, Adobe Stock 
 Donald Trump ’s hatred of election projections that make him or his allies look bad runs so deep he has sued over it.
 At the same time, his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., is invested in prediction market companies currently making him look terrible.
 Trump Jr.- backed exchange operators Kalshi and Polymarket allow people to wager on election results, with their live odds offering a snapshot of how the U.S. views politicians at any given moment. After they flattered Trump ahead of the 2024 presidential election, leading Trump to praise prediction markets as better than “fake polls,” their outlooks for Republicans have turned dire entering Tuesday’s midterms.
 Democrats hold a higher than 70% chance to win control of the House and Senate, per Kalshi at noon on Monday, way up from four months ago when the odds of the party taking control of both chambers sat below 40%.
 The shift puts prediction market firms in an awkward spot. They need Trump’s support amid what Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour has called a “brutal, bloody war” against states and tribal groups that want the industry regulated and taxed like gambling rather than as a financial asset class.
 So far during Trump’s second term, prediction markets have received favorable treatment from Trump-appointed Commodity Futures Trading Commission ( CFTC ) chairman Michael Selig. The federal agency provides safe harbor from state gambling laws—a sharp contrast to how the CFTC handled things under Joe Biden—and has taken an active role in litigation on the side of Kalshi and Polymarket.
 Selig interprets his role atop the CFTC as “serving President Donald J. Trump,” according to his X bio, aligning his regulatory actions with White House desires. He keeps a red “Make America Great Again” hat on a shelf behind him for many video interviews with news publications. His chief of staff Alex Titus previously worked for America First Action, a pro-Trump Super PAC, according to LinkedIn.
 There’s no guarantee Trump will notice or care about prediction markets this week. It’s also possible the odds will change dramatically in Republicans’ favor over the next 24 hours.
 But if Trump does turn against the sector for the same reason he fumes at polls, it would pressure Selig to adjust how the CFTC handles prediction markets.
 Kalshi declined to comment. Polymarket, the CFTC and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.
 Ducking Donald 
 Election projections are a sore spot for Trump. For years, he has seethed at traditional polls that anticipate him or his allies underperforming.
 Trump sued pollster J. Ann Selzer for a 2024 Iowa poll she released just before he defeated Joe Biden to re-take the White House. Not even Trump’s election victory cushioned Selzer from his fury, though the dismissal of his case in October by Iowa District Judge Scott J. Beattie provided Selzer some reprieve.
 Trump’s frustrations toward polls have remained high in the build-up to midterms.
 “Don’t believe the Radical Left’s Fake Poll numbers,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Aug. 3. “They are Crooked and Corrupt, just like the Country Destroying Dumocrats are Crooked and Corrupt.”
 There’s no surefire way for prediction markets to avoid Trump’s naughty list this week.
 Many TV networks, including Fox, CNN and CNBC, will incorporate live odds in their election night broadcasts. Kalshi and Polymarket upped the chances of Trump noticing their election prognostications when they partnered with those media companies amid an aggressive push to attract new bettors. Polymarket also has a deal with The Wall Street Journal .
 Managing the optics 
 On the other hand, embarking on a full-court press to keep Trump and his family happy right now would come with its own risks as exchange operators increasingly consider how Democrats perceive them.
 Should Democrats blow out Republicans on Tuesday like prediction market users anticipate they will, the caucus could use its increased power to press Kalshi and Polymarket for internal records related to their financial ties to Trump’s family and probe their election integrity safeguards and marketing practices .
 Already, Democrats have signaled they intend to hold hearings with Trump-aligned groups on Capitol Hill if they gain power through the midterms—not just with prediction market firms, but also with companies involved with crypto and AI.
 “Control of Congress could reset the playing field,” Seeking Alpha wrote in an analyst note this weekend. “The effort to restrict prediction markets from offering sports contracts could move forward if the Democrats control the House of Representatives, while a majority in the Senate would likely put Elizabeth Warren, a prediction market skeptic, in charge of the Senate Banking Committee.”
 Throughout this year, Kalshi has hired people with close connections to former President Barack Obama, a Democrat who Trump despises and who still holds significant sway with his party. Companies across North America that bent to Trump’s will earlier in his second term have made similar liberal-leaning appointments of late in an apparent effort to minimize Congressional scrutiny from Democrats in the event the party takes control of one or both chambers.
 Kalshi last week added ex-Obama deputy White House press secretary Eric Schultz as an advisor. That’s after appointing former Obama and Biden campaign staffer John Bivona as head of government relations in January and onboarding former Obama campaign manager Stephanie Cutter as an advisor in April.
 Still, the firm has introduced some more Trump-connected Republicans, including Jacki McGavick, Trump’s former policy communications director who Kalshi hired in June to help with public relations.
 Despite the Trump administration’s full-throated support for prediction markets to date and prominent Democrats like Warren bashing the industry, prediction markets are not a clear-cut partisan issue.
 Utah and Montana are among the Republican-controlled states in active litigation against operators. Democrat-led California, meanwhile, has yet to file a lawsuit against a prediction market platform or send anyone a cease-and-desist order, though it joined 36 other state attorneys general last week in signing an amicus brief supporting Utah in its legal battle with Kalshi.
 Frustrations around election markets already bu b bled during U.S. primaries this spring and exploded around international elections in Romania and Colombia. Some observers blamed the exchanges for influencing voter behavior, while others accused them of stoking conspiracies.
 Credibility test 
 Sports betting is by far the top revenue driver for prediction markets, but their original purpose derives from forecasting elections. As Kalshi and Polymarket argue they offer utility as a “truth machine,” a strong performance in the midterms would boost their forecasting credibility, even if questions about their impact on the election process might linger.
 Past academic studies suggest prediction markets are susceptible to a long-shot bias, meaning massive underdogs hold slightly more optimistic odds than results indicate they should. But data shows that even with this skew, prediction markets have historically been well-calibrated within the year an election occurs (far in advance markets are much less accurate).
 Candidates with 30% prediction market odds of winning an election have typically won about 30% of the time. Of course, that’s over a large sample size.
 This will likely be the highest-volume election betting week in world history, providing researchers a fresh and robust set of data points to dissect. It is possible new biases could emerge.
 Kalshi and Polymarket have been frustrated by the public’s recent tendency to pick out election upsets like the one in Brazil last month as proof prediction markets are broken, regardless of their calibration across multiple election cycles.
 Some of the blame for this interpretation falls on the companies. For more than a year, Kalshi and Polymarket claimed the outcome of the 2024 presidential election showed their exchanges were “right.” In reality, no single event can prove an entire probability model right or wrong.
 Mansour acknowledged this as a PR misstep last week, writing on X that his company “got too excited” in its previous framing. It might be too late. The surprise Brazil result last month was part of a spree of unexpected overseas election outcomes in 2026, which has increased scrutiny and sometimes derision of prediction markets’ reliability.
 Fair or not, Kalshi and Polymarket will face public mockery if Democrats flop Tuesday.
 That alone wouldn’t necessarily be catastrophic—prediction market operators have shown they can withstand substantial public anger . In a sign of investors being able to tune out naysayers, Kalshi just completed a raise at a $40 billion valuation, having only crossed $1 billion in the summer of 2025.
 Anger from Trump, though, could prove more difficult to handle—and Trump appears to be in a combustible state with his party at risk of losing its Congressional edge.
 “They’re just liars,” Trump said at a Kansas rally on Sunday about those who highlight his declining public perception . “They’re really dishonest people. … Honestly, they’re the biggest threat to our country.”
